read.sections.0.heading.source: Schools are deciding how to use AI
read.sections.0.heading.back: Schools are deciding how to use AI

read.sections.0.text.source: AI chat tools can answer questions, explain ideas and even write whole essays. So schools and families face a new question: how should students use them? In 2023, UNESCO, the United Nations organisation for education, asked more than 450 schools and universities. Fewer than 1 in 10 had any guidance about these tools. Later that year, UNESCO wrote guidance for governments. It asked them to protect students' privacy and to set a minimum age, such as 13, for children talking with these chat tools on their own. This is advice, not a law. Each country and school makes its own rules.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI chat tools can answer questions, explain ideas and even write whole essays. So schools and families face a new question: how should students use these tools? In 2023 UNESCO, the United Nations organisation for education, asked more than 450 schools and universities. Fewer than 1 in 10 had guidance about these tools. Later the same year UNESCO wrote guidance for governments, asking them to protect students' privacy and set a minimum age, such as 13 for children who talk with these chat tools on their own. This is advice, not law; each country and each school sets its own rules.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Nigeria: an AI tutor with teachers in the room
read.sections.1.heading.back: Nigeria: an AI tutor with a teacher in the room

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2024, World Bank researchers tested an AI tutor in nine state schools in Benin City, Nigeria. The students were in their first year of senior secondary school, usually about 15 years old. For six weeks, they came to computer rooms after school, twice a week, to practise English with an AI chat tool. Teachers trained for the project started each session with a first question to ask the tool. Then they walked around, helping students stay on task. At the end, these students did better on an English test than similar students who were not chosen. The researchers say the result came from the whole programme, the tool and the teachers together.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2024 World Bank researchers tested an AI tutor in nine state schools in Benin City, Nigeria. The students were in the first year of upper secondary school, usually about 15 years old. For six weeks they came to the computer room after school twice a week to practise English with an AI chat tool. Teachers trained for this programme began each session with a first question for students to ask the tool. Then the teachers walked around the room and helped students keep working. At the end of the programme these students did better on an English test than similar students who were not chosen. The researchers say this result came from the whole programme: the tool and the teachers working together.
read.sections.1.text.note: Benin City = เมืองเบนินซิตี; World Bank = ธนาคารโลก; "session" = คาบ (KEY_TERMS: คาบเรียน); "first year of senior secondary school" = ชั้นปีแรกของมัธยมศึกษาตอนปลาย. "Students" = นักเรียน in this lesson, because it is about school (KEY_TERMS keeps ผู้เรียน for Thinkerwell's learners).

read.sections.2.heading.source: Türkiye: practice with a tool is not the same as learning
read.sections.2.heading.back: Türkiye: practising with a tool is not the same as learning
read.sections.2.heading.note: Türkiye = ทูร์เคีย, the name the Thai government has used since 2022, to match the English. Many Thai readers still say ตุรกี; a reviewer should choose. Not in KEY_TERMS.

read.sections.2.text.source: In 2023, researchers worked with nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at a high school in Türkiye. In four maths lessons, a teacher reviewed a topic, students did practice problems, and then they took a test with no books or computers. During practice, some students had only their books. Some had a chat tool that could give full answers. Others had a tutor version that gave hints, using answers and common mistakes written by their teachers. Both AI groups did much better in practice. But on the test alone, the full-answer group did worse than the books-only group. The tool had become a shortcut. The hint group did about as well as the books-only group. Each study was one subject in one place, so results elsewhere may differ.
read.sections.2.text.back: In 2023 researchers worked with almost 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at a high school in Türkiye. In four maths lessons the teacher reviewed a topic, students did practice problems, then took a test without books or computers. During practice some students had only books, some had a chat tool that could give full answers, and others had a different kind of tutor that gave hints using answers and common mistakes their teachers had written. Both AI groups did much better in practice. But in the test they had to do alone, the full-answer group did worse than the books-only group: the tool had become a shortcut. The hint group did about as well as the books-only group. Each study looked at one subject in one place, so results elsewhere may differ.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Another study was in Türkiye, with nearly 1,000 high school students. In four maths lessons, students did practice problems. Then they took a test with no help. Some practised with only books. Some had a chat tool that gave full answers. Others had a tool that gave hints. Their teachers helped to make it. Both tool groups did well in practice. On the test alone, the full-answer group did worse. The tool was a shortcut. The hint group did about the same as the books group. Each study was one subject in one place.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Another study was done in Türkiye with almost 1,000 high school students. In four maths lessons students did practice problems, then took a test without help. Some practised with books only. Some had a chat tool that gave full answers. Others had a tool that gave hints; their teachers helped build it. Both tool groups did well in practice. In the test they did alone, the full-answer group did worse. The tool was a shortcut. The hint group did as well as the book group. Each study looked at one subject in one place.

watch.summary.source: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program you can chat with in writing. It is a bit like sending messages to a person. The video explains what chatbots are and how they work. It also asks why many of them are made to sound like people. A chatbot can sound friendly and human. This can make it feel like a friend. It can also make its answers feel more true than they are. But a chatbot is not a person. It does not really know you, and it can be wrong. So notice how a chatbot makes you feel. And check what it says before you trust it.
watch.summary.back: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program you can type to, like sending messages to a person. The video explains what chatbots are and how they work, and also asks why many chatbots are made to talk like people. A chatbot may sound friendly and human, which can make it feel like a friend and can make its answers seem more believable than they really are. But a chatbot is not a person. It does not really know you, and it can answer wrongly. So notice how a chatbot makes you feel, and check what it says before believing it.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Don't ask learners whether or how they have used AI tools for schoolwork, and don't ask them to type questions into a real AI tool in class. UNESCO's 2023 guidance asks governments to set an age limit for children's independent conversations with generative AI tools; its press release names 13, and news reports said some argue for 16. It is advice to governments, not a law or a rule for every learning tool, and many learners are younger than 13. The pretend tool keeps everyone offline.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Do not ask learners whether or how they have used AI tools for homework, and do not ask learners to type questions into a real AI tool in class. UNESCO's 2023 guidance asks governments to set a minimum age for children talking with generative AI tools alone; the press release gives 13, and news reported some proposing 16. This is advice to governments, not a law or a rule for all learning tools, and many learners are under 13. The pretend tool keeps everyone offline.

educatorNotes.1.source: The two studies, simplified (claims/DW11.md). Nigeria (De Simone and others, World Bank, 2025): a randomised trial in nine public schools in Benin City, Edo State, June to July 2024, with first-year senior secondary students (typically 15). Students chosen at random could attend twelve 90-minute after-school sessions (at most two a week) using Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4). Teachers had three days' training, began each session with a prompt, guided students without teaching directly and circulated to keep them on task; monitors supervised the sessions. On a pen-and-paper test at the end, gains were 0.31 standard deviations overall and 0.23 on English, with better end-of-year exams too. The authors say the whole programme, tool and teacher guidance together, drove the result; they can't separate the AI's part from the teacher guidance, and don't know how long it lasts or whether it works in other subjects. Türkiye (Bastani and others, PNAS 2025; design from the 2024 working paper): nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at one large high school, autumn 2023; four 90-minute sessions covering about 15% of the year's maths; the AI was available only during practice, with a teacher present. With GPT-4 in practice, grades rose 48% (plain chat tool) and 127% (hint tutor built with teachers' solutions and common mistakes); on the closed-book test afterwards, the plain-tool group scored 17% lower than the books-only group, and the tutor group about the same. Neither study shows an effect for every learner, subject or tool.
educatorNotes.1.back: The two studies in brief (claims/DW11.md). Nigeria (De Simone et al., World Bank, 2025): a randomised trial in nine state schools in Benin City, Edo State, June to July 2024, with first-year upper secondary students (usually 15). Randomly chosen students could attend twelve 90-minute after-school sessions (at most two a week) using Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4). Teachers had three days' training, began each session with a starting prompt, guided students without teaching directly, and walked around to keep students working; monitors oversaw sessions. On a paper test at the end, results rose 0.31 standard deviations overall and 0.23 in English, and end-of-year exam results also improved. The authors say the whole programme, tool and teacher guidance together, drove the results; they cannot separate the AI's part from the teacher guidance, and do not know how long effects last or whether they apply to other subjects. Türkiye (Bastani et al., PNAS 2025; design from the 2024 paper): almost 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at one large high school, autumn 2023, four 90-minute sessions covering about 15 percent of the year's maths. AI was available only during practice, with teachers present. With GPT-4 in practice, scores rose 48 percent (plain chat tool) and 127 percent (hint tutor built from teachers' solutions and common mistakes). In the closed-book test afterwards, the plain-tool group scored 17 percent lower than the books-only group, and the tutor group about the same. No study shows results for all learners, subjects or tools.
